result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.to_nested_tuple()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Encode an undirected tree, hanging from root=, as nested tuples. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.to_nested_tuple()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Encode an undirected tree, hanging from root=, as nested tuples. title: >- [Graph.to_nested_tuple()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- Encode an undirected tree, hanging from root=, as nested tuples. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Encode an undirected tree, hanging from `root=`, as nested tuples. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L70322-L70439){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.to_nested_tuple( root, canonical_form=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![To nested tuple](../assets/graphs/to-nested-tuple.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A tree rooted at A, outlined in the accent color, with children B, C and D. B has two leaf children E and F, drawn in teal; C is a leaf, in violet; D has one leaf child G, in gold. The card writes each child's subtree as a tuple of its children's tuples, in the same colors: B is ((), ()), C is () and D is ((),). Together they give the result (((), ()), (), ((),))." width="100%"} The nested tuple code describes the *shape* of a rooted tree without its labels: a leaf is the empty tuple `()`, and a node with `k` children is the tuple of its `k` children's codes. So a root with two leaf children is `((), ())`, and a path of three nodes read from one end is `(((),),)`. The code is a plain Python value, handy for printing, hashing and comparing tree shapes, and `Graph.from_nested_tuple()` turns it back into a tree. By default the children appear in ascending order of node ID. With `canonical_form=True`, the children of every node are sorted by their own codes instead, so two rooted trees get the same code exactly when they are isomorphic (the same shape, whatever the labels). That turns rooted tree isomorphism into an equality test and makes the code usable as a dictionary key. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [root]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node (ID or label) to hang the tree from. [canonical_form]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, sort the children of every node by their codes, giving a canonical code for the rooted tree. If `False` (the default), children follow ascending node ID. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [tuple]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The nested tuple code of the tree rooted at `root=`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed or not a tree, or `root=` is not in the graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} One breadth-first pass from the root finds every node's children, and the codes are then assembled bottom-up, so deep trees (long paths) cause no recursion. Sorting for the canonical form compares tuples lexicographically, with shorter tuples first on a common prefix, which is the AHU-style encoding behind linear-time rooted tree isomorphism. NetworkX visits children in set order, which for integer node labels is ascending, so on such trees the default code matches NetworkX's. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Hang a small tree from A: B has two leaves below it, C is a leaf, and D has one: ::: {#84990016 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec t = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G"]) t.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("A", "D"), ("B", "E"), ("B", "F"), ("D", "G")]) t.to_nested_tuple("A") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (((), ()), (), ((),)) ``` ::: ::: The canonical form sorts every list of children, lighter subtrees first: ::: {#e337aa91 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} t.to_nested_tuple("A", canonical_form=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ((), ((),), ((), ())) ``` ::: ::: The same tree hung from a different node has a different shape: ::: {#68233e7e .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} t.to_nested_tuple("G") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (((((), ()), ()),),) ``` ::: ::: Two differently labeled trees with the same rooted shape get equal canonical codes: ::: {#33110fe9 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} u = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["r", "x", "y", "z", "w", "v", "q"]) u.add_edges([("r", "x"), ("r", "y"), ("r", "z"), ("y", "w"), ("z", "v"), ("z", "q")]) u.to_nested_tuple("r", canonical_form=True) == t.to_nested_tuple("A", canonical_form=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` True ``` ::: :::
